description: Databases make decisions too: IF and CASE for branching, LOOP / WHILE / FOR for repeating, and cursors for walking through rows one at a time.

screens.body: Databases need to make decisions just like apps do. IF checks a condition and picks a path; ELSIF chains more checks; ELSE catches everything left. The condition usually involves data — is this order over $100? is the account active? Same if/else brain, database body.

options: Picks a path based on a data condition
check.question: An IF block…

screens.heading: IF: the bouncer
screens.keyPoint: IF / ELSIF / ELSE — decisions driven by data.

screens.body: When one value could be many things, CASE is cleaner than a ladder of ELSIFs. Simple CASE matches a value against options; searched CASE checks full conditions. It reads like a menu: 'for THIS, do THAT.' You'll see it inside SELECTs too — it's one of the most-used database constructs there is.

options: It matches one value against many options cleanly
check.question: Why reach for CASE over a long IF/ELSIF chain?

code.snippet:
v_tier := CASE
  WHEN v_points >= 1000 THEN 'gold'
  WHEN v_points >= 500  THEN 'silver'
  ELSE 'bronze'
END;

screens.heading: CASE: the menu
screens.keyPoint: CASE matches one value against many outcomes — clean and readable.

screens.body: The plain LOOP just repeats until you tell it to stop — and you stop it with EXIT WHEN. Forget the exit and it spins forever, burning through the database. It's the most explicit loop: you control exactly when it ends, which is powerful and slightly dangerous.

check.question: How do you get out of a LOOP?

screens.heading: LOOP: repeat until told to stop
screens.keyPoint: LOOP needs EXIT WHEN, or it never stops.

screens.body: Two loops with training wheels. WHILE repeats as long as a condition is true — the check happens before each round. FOR counts through a range for you — FOR i IN 1..10 runs exactly 10 times, and you don't even declare i. When you know the shape of the repetition, these are safer than a bare LOOP.

options: FOR declares and counts for you — no manual exit needed
check.question: FOR i IN 1..10 beats a manual LOOP because…

screens.heading: WHILE and FOR: loops with training wheels
screens.keyPoint: WHILE checks a condition; FOR counts a range for you.

screens.body: Here's the big one: a cursor is a pointer to a set of rows. You OPEN it (run the query), FETCH rows one at a time into variables, and CLOSE it when done. The loop usually exits WHEN cursor%NOTFOUND — 'no more rows.' Cursors are how database code processes rows individually instead of all at once.

options: OPEN, FETCH one at a time, CLOSE
SELECT everything into memory at once
check.question: The cursor lifecycle is…

screens.heading: Cursors: walking rows one at a time

screens.body: Time to combine the moves: loop through rows with a cursor, and let IF/CASE decide what happens to each one. This is the classic data-driven flow — the same pattern behind nightly jobs like 'find every overdue order and flag it.' Loop gives you each row; conditionals give each row its fate.

options: The loop fetches rows, the IF decides each row's fate
The IF fetches rows, the loop decides
check.question: In a cursor loop with an IF inside…

screens.heading: Putting it together: loop + decide
screens.keyPoint: Cursor FOR loop + IF inside = the classic data-driven flow.

screens.body: Two ways to ruin your afternoon. One: a LOOP with no EXIT WHEN — it spins forever, and the database will happily burn CPU until someone kills it. Two: opening a cursor and never closing it — leaked cursors pile up and the database starts refusing new ones. Rule of thumb: every LOOP gets an exit, every OPEN gets a CLOSE. (Cursor FOR loops do both for you — one more reason to love them.)

options: Every LOOP gets an exit; every OPEN gets a CLOSE
Never use loops in a database
Always use WHILE instead of FOR

screens.heading: Watch out: the infinite loop
screens.keyPoint: No EXIT WHEN = infinite loop. No CLOSE = leaked cursor.
